title: Getting Confucius Wrong
gist: A scholar of ancient Chinese manuscripts argues Erin Cline's new translation of the Analects fails by ignoring two millennia of scholarship and recent archaeological manuscript finds, using this critique to warn that oversimplified handling of foundational Chinese texts reflects Washington's broader, decades-long failure to genuinely understand Chinese culture.

themes.theme: Confucius as instrument of state power

insights.claim: Xi Jinping and other Chinese leaders often promote the Analects, and the PRC runs worldwide Confucius Institutes to study Chinese culture—even though the PRC viciously attacked Confucianism for three decades after its 1949 founding.
insights.speaker: Maddalena Poli
insights.so_what: Beijing's instrumental revival of a tradition it once persecuted illustrates how the CCP repurposes cultural heritage for soft-power projection—context for reading Confucius Institutes as statecraft.
insights.quote: the People’s Republic of China promotes its own worldwide Confucius Institutes for studying Chinese culture –even though it viciously attacked Confucianism for three decades after its foundation
insights.locator: Confucius and the Analects became foundational aspects

insights.claim: The author frames understanding ancient Chinese texts as an important part of understanding Chinese culture and scholarship—'something Washington has notably failed at for decades'—linking scholarly rigor to strategic competence.
insights.speaker: Maddalena Poli
insights.so_what: Argues U.S. cultural illiteracy about China is a strategic liability, a soft-power/intelligence gap relevant to how well Washington reads Beijing.
insights.quote: Understanding ancient Chinese texts is an important part of understanding Chinese culture and scholarship—something Washington has notably failed at for decades.

insights.claim: Cline's translation claims to correct inaccuracies about women (e.g. via Analects 8.20) but ignores centuries of commentary—including Ma Rong and Zheng Xuan's reading that a scribal error swapped 'Yin person' for 'woman'—and a 2019 Hubei tomb manuscript indicating the passage merged distinct sayings.
insights.speaker: Maddalena Poli
insights.so_what: Shows how a headline 'corrective' reading collapses once the full textual record is consulted—a caution on trusting simplified reinterpretations of primary sources.
insights.quote: At some point the character for “woman” was mistakenly used in place of the character for “Yin,” the type of error that was common in the world before print.

insights.claim: Cline's books contain no citations from Chinese sources and omit standard commentarial editions and key gender scholarship (Kinney, Rosenlee, Milburn), while claiming to uncover the story of Nanzi 'for the first time' despite prior studies.
insights.speaker: Maddalena Poli
insights.so_what: Documents an expertise gap in a widely marketed translation, a case study in how popularization can misrepresent a field's actual state of knowledge.
insights.quote: There are no citations from Chinese sources
insights.locator: Errors of this kind would have been avoided

insights.claim: Recent decades of Chinese archaeology have recovered manuscripts from tombs sealed in the last centuries B.C. that offer priceless access to ancient languages and writing habits, making proper handling of the Analects' textual formation mandatory for any translation.
insights.speaker: Maddalena Poli
insights.so_what: New manuscript evidence is actively rewriting the textual history of foundational Chinese classics—a reminder that the scholarly baseline on China is a moving target.
insights.quote: the process of uncovering the textual history of the Analects remains ongoing
